Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Weight-Tied Transformers on Depth-Bound Algorithmic Tasks

Magnus Sesodia Affiliation: University of Oxford    Juil Sock Affiliation: BBC R&D    Philip Torr Affiliation: University of Oxford    Christian Schroeder de Witt Affiliation: University of Oxford
Abstract

Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows HH hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically-trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.

1 Introduction

Looped transformers have become an active front in latent reasoning thanks to their ability to scale computation without adding parameters or tokens. Where an untied transformer passes each input through its stack of layers just once (T=1T=1), a looped model passes it T≥2T\geq 2 times by feeding the hidden state at the end of each iteration back to the start, multiplying the effective depth by TT. While the idea of a depth-recurrent transformer is not new (Dehghani et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2020), it had been sitting largely dormant until recent strong performance at multi-billion-parameter scale (Geiping et al., 2025; Zhu et al., 2025) brought this paradigm back into the spotlight, triggering a proliferation of work spanning new variants, scaling laws and theory.

The most obvious benefit of looping is parameter efficiency, since a block reused TT times occupies a TT-th of the storage of an untied stack of the same depth. A second advantage is latent bandwidth, since looped models reason exclusively in hidden states, which forgoes the need to throttle intermediate computation into discrete chain-of-thought tokens (Xu and Sato, 2026; Hao et al., 2025). But the strength of looped models which we investigate in this paper is their purported inductive bias toward iterative computation (Saunshi et al., 2025; Giannou et al., 2023). Logically, weight tying should favor the learning of a repeated function, predisposing looped models to multi-hop reasoning and step-by-step algorithms. Yet it is unclear whether a looped model actually runs such an algorithm, advancing the solution by one step per iteration, or merely simulates a deeper untied stack with fewer parameters. The distinction matters for model design, since if the loop runs an algorithm, its iteration budget sets how many steps each iteration must take. So far, mechanistic studies of hidden-state trajectories have not settled this question (Lu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026; Blayney et al., 2026; Curth et al., 2026), in part because natural text offers no ground truth for intermediate states.

We work in a controlled setting using directed permutation traversal (dePo), a task from the physics-of-LMs lineage (Allen-Zhu and Li, 2025; Ye et al., 2025) akin to the knowledge-graph walks that Kohli et al. (2026) use to study recurrent-depth transformers. Here, the model is presented with the edges of a cycle of NN nodes in shuffled order and reports the node reached after HH hops from a given start node (Figure 2). This gives us a clear difficulty knob in the number of hops required HH and, crucially, every intermediate hop hh has a known node. Thus, we can ask not just whether the final answer is correct but where in the network each intermediate node becomes decodable, although none is ever supervised. This separates the two explanations, as an iterative algorithm predicts that the state after iteration tt encodes hop tt, while a simulated deep stack need not tie nodes to iterations.

We begin by asking: do looped models outperform untied models at matched effective depth? If they do, a natural explanation is that weight tying steers training toward an iterative algorithm, in which one update is reused at every iteration. Such an algorithm should leave evidence in the model’s intermediate states, motivating the follow-up question: does each loop iteration advance the computation by a fixed number of hops? We answer it using linear probes on the hidden state after every layer, the model’s own logit lens and activation patching.

Contributions.

  1. 1.

    Looped models are better learners. We show that, trained identically at matched effective depth, looped models solve the task where untied models do not, even with eight times the parameters. Untied models need a lower learning rate or auxiliary supervision (§4).

  2. 2.

    Looped models build a staircase (and use it). We find that looped models advance the computation gradually with each iteration (Figure 1), at a rate set by the iteration budget, without any intermediate supervision. The untied models we probe that solve the task show no such staircase unless their intermediate layers are supervised. Activation patching shows that the patched state decides which walk the model finishes (§5).

2 Related Work

Looped architectures.

Universal Transformers (Dehghani et al., 2019) were the first to introduce the concept of a depth-recurrent transformer equipped with an adaptive halting mechanism Graves, 2016; Banino et al., 2021. Beyond parameter efficiency (Lan et al., 2020), looping can turn even a shallow transformer into a programmable computer (Giannou et al., 2023) and may bias learning toward iterative algorithms (Yang et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025). More recently, at-scale work has established looped models as competitive on downstream reasoning benchmarks, looping either a middle block between an untied prelude and coda (Geiping et al., 2025; Prairie et al., 2026; McLeish et al., 2026), termed middle-cycle sharing by Bae et al. (2025b), or the full stack (Zhu et al., 2025; Bae et al., 2025a; Gao et al., 2025). Other variants add elastic depth (Jeddi et al., 2026), multi-resolution recursion (Yu et al., 2026), per-token adaptive depth (Bae et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025), iteration-aware conditioning (Xu and Sato, 2025), hierarchical recurrence (Wang et al., 2025) and hyper-connected residual streams (Zeitoun et al., 2026), skip or repeat pretrained layers (Li et al., 2025) or stabilize many-step recurrence (Chen, 2026). Iso-depth scaling laws also measure what one extra iteration is worth in added layers (Schwethelm et al., 2026). Ours is the simplest case, sharing every layer with an iteration encoding and no prelude, coda or input injection, to isolate the loop.

Theory and dynamics.

Theory shows that a looped transformer can nearly match an untied model of the same effective depth (Saunshi et al., 2025) and solve graph reachability where constant depth fails (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2025), and it formally separates looped computation from chain of thought (Xu and Sato, 2026), yet expressivity alone cannot tell whether a trained loop runs an iterative algorithm or simulates the deeper stack. Viewed as a dynamical system, a weight-tied layer can be solved directly for its fixed point (Bai et al., 2019), long recurrences need stabilizing (Prairie et al., 2026), and trained looped models converge to cyclic fixed points that repeat the stages of feedforward inference (Blayney et al., 2026), with two-scale dynamics (Pappone et al., 2025) shared by depth-grown models (Kapl et al., 2026). These studies describe where the trajectory goes, while decoding Huginn-3.5B’s iterations with the logit lens finds only limited evidence of a per-iteration chain (Lu et al., 2025). Untied transformers instead spread step-by-step search across layers and struggle to learn it (Saparov et al., 2025; Brinkmann et al., 2024; Biran et al., 2024), the contrast our comparison at matched effective depth isolates.

Closest work.

Kohli et al. (2026) study recurrent-depth transformers on multi-relation knowledge-graph walks, and we differ in task (single-permutation dePo with every edge in the prompt), training and per-iteration probing. Concurrently, Zhang et al. (2026) find on group word problems that weight tying installs a serial computation frontier resolving a fixed number of positions per loop, at a rate set by the training budget, which corroborates the per-loop rate we read from the hidden states (§5).

3 Methods

3.1 Task: directed permutation traversal

We focus on directed permutation traversal (dePo, Figure 2), a controlled depth-bound algorithmic task in the physics-of-LMs lineage (Allen-Zhu, 2025). A random permutation π\pi over N=16N=16 nodes is sampled uniformly from the single NN-cycles and presented to the model as an explicit edge list in shuffled order, followed by a query with a start node ss and a hop count HH whose answer is πH​(s)\pi^{H}(s), the node HH steps along the cycle. Since every hop depends on the result of the previous one, any correct walk visits the intermediate reference states zh=πh​(s)z_{h}=\pi^{h}(s) for h∈{1,…,H−1}h\in\{1,\ldots,H-1\}, whose known ground truth lets us ask where in the network each one becomes decodable (§3.4). We train and evaluate on H∈{1,…,15}H\in\{1,\ldots,15\}, and five queries share the edge list of each prompt.

Because the cycle closes, HH forward hops reach the same node as N−HN-H backward hops, so a query needs at most min⁡(H,N−H)≤8\min(H,N-H)\leq 8 sequential steps and we analyse internal states at H≤8H\leq 8. We check that the 2×162\times 16 model walks forward where the backward walk is shorter (App. C, Fig. A3) and repeat the capability comparison at N=32N=32, where any H≤15H\leq 15 takes HH steps (§4).

3.2 Looped and untied models

A looped transformer reuses the same block of LL decoder layers across TT iterations, and we write L×TL\times T for such a model. With fθf_{\theta} an LL-layer block with parameters θ\theta and x(0)x^{(0)} the embedded input tokens, the two families compute

looped:x(t)\displaystyle\text{looped:}\quad x^{(t)} =fθ​(x(t−1)+τt),\displaystyle=f_{\theta}\bigl(x^{(t-1)}+\tau_{t}\bigr), (1)
untied:x(t)\displaystyle\text{untied:}\quad x^{(t)} =fθt​(x(t−1)),\displaystyle=f_{\theta_{t}}\bigl(x^{(t-1)}\bigr), (2)

for t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T, where τt\tau_{t} is a learnable iteration embedding (Dehghani et al., 2019; Xu and Sato, 2025) (ablated in App. C), and an unembedding head is then applied to x(T)x^{(T)}. Per forward pass both perform Deff=L​TD_{\mathrm{eff}}=LT layer evaluations, the effective depth, but the untied model stacks L​TLT distinct layers applied once, so we call it the untied L​TLT-layer model and place it at T=1T=1 in Figure 3. That figure covers effective depths from 22 to 3232, with looped blocks of L∈{2,4,8,16}L\in\{2,4,8,16\} layers iterated up to T=16T=16 times and untied models of 22 to 3232 layers. Both families are decoder-only with width d=256d=256, 88 heads, pre-norm RMSNorm, SwiGLU MLPs and rotary position embeddings (RoPE), and neither uses adaptive halting (Graves, 2016; Banino et al., 2021), input re-injection or intermediate readouts, so the two families differ mainly in how many distinct layers fill the same number of layer evaluations. Besides weight tying, the looped model alone adds iteration embeddings and zero-initializes the output projections of its attention and MLP sublayers (Kohli et al., 2026), and at matched DeffD_{\mathrm{eff}} it has about TT times fewer parameters, e.g., 3.223.22M for the 4×84\times 8 model against 25.7225.72M for the untied 3232-layer model.

3.3 Training and evaluation

All models are trained from scratch for 100100k steps with AdamW at peak learning rate η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} unless stated otherwise, with five seeds per configuration (App. A). The loss is next-token cross-entropy on every non-pad token of the prompt, read out from the final layer only, so no intermediate hop is ever supervised. A hop curriculum holds H=1H=1 for the first 77k steps and then widens the range of sampled hop lengths linearly to H≤15H\leq 15 by step 3030k, after which every batch covers all 1515 hop lengths uniformly. Section 4 also trains the looped 4×84\times 8 and the untied models at η=3×10−4\eta=3\times 10^{-4} and 10−410^{-4}, and, in one variant, adds the same next-token loss at the outputs of layers 88, 1616 and 2424 of the untied 3232-layer model, read out through the shared final RMSNorm and unembedding with a total weight of 0.30.3. At N=32N=32 we train three seeds per model at η=3×10−4\eta=3\times 10^{-4} with a 384384-token context. On trained models we score the first query of each prompt, and an answer counts as correct only if every digit and the delimiter that follows it are correct under teacher forcing, so always writing the same node scores 1/161/16. The evaluations every 44k steps during training instead score the digits of the last query, whose earlier queries share HH and can repeat its start node, so a model that copies earlier answers scores about 0.360.36 on this measure (App. A). A seed solves the task when its final training-time evaluation reaches accuracy 0.80.8 on every hop length from 11 to 1515, and its solved-chain depth H⋆H^{\star} is the largest HH such that every hop length up to HH reaches 0.80.8 on that evaluation.

3.4 Probes, logit lens and activation patching

Linear probes.

For every depth ℓ\ell and hop hh, we train a linear classifier to decode the reference state zhz_{h} from the residual stream at the position just before the answer, i.e., the space token after the question mark, which predicts the answer’s first digit. We read the state after every layer, so layer ℓ\ell of an L×TL\times T model ends iteration ℓ/L\ell/L, e.g., layer 88 of the 4×84\times 8 model ends iteration 22. The probes use the five queries of 5,0005{,}000 fresh prompts, split by prompt into 4,0004{,}000 for fitting and 1,0001{,}000 held out, so no permutation appears on both sides. As the headline quantity we use probe selectivity (Hewitt and Liang, 2019), Sℓ,h=Accreal​(ℓ,h)−Accshuffled​(ℓ,h)S_{\ell,h}=\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{real}}(\ell,h)-\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{shuffled}}(\ell,h), the gain in held-out accuracy over a control probe fitted to shuffled labels, which approaches one for a linearly readable node and zero otherwise. A hop counts as decodable wherever Sℓ,h≥0.5S_{\ell,h}\geq 0.5, and the first depth at which it does is its onset. The untied maps at η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} (Figure 4b,d) and the forward-walk control use an earlier split by query row (App. B).

Logit lens and activation patching.

To see what the model would write after tt iterations, we stop the loop there and apply its own final RMSNorm and unembedding head (nostalgebraist, 2020), scoring each node in full as the probability of all its digits and the delimiter, so the lens has no learned readout and reproduces the model’s answers at t=Tt=T (App. B). To check that the model relies on these states, we replace the receiver’s states at its two answer positions after iteration tt with those of a donor prompt that shares the permutation but starts from a different node, and let the remaining iterations finish (Figure 6c). An untrained model serves as the control, and App. C repeats the patching with a donor that has a different permutation and the same start node.

4 Looped models are better learners

So why does looping work? The simplest hypothesis is that looping buys effective depth, and that this depth alone explains the additional capability. If so, an LL-layer model looped TT times and an untied L​TLT-layer model should perform about the same and, if anything, the untied model should hold a slight advantage, since it has TT times the parameters and so can express a much larger function class. We put this to the test by jointly varying LL and TT at several fixed values of DeffD_{\mathrm{eff}}, following the setup of Saunshi et al. (2025).

Effective depth is necessary but not sufficient

We find, emphatically, that effective depth alone cannot predict model capability. This is clear when comparing models along any diagonal of constant DeffD_{\mathrm{eff}} in Figure 3. For example, at Deff=32D_{\mathrm{eff}}=32 (the rightmost diagonal), the 8×48\times 4, 4×84\times 8 and 2×162\times 16 looped models solve the task in at least four of five seeds, while the untied 3232-layer model and the 16×216\times 2 model, which loops only twice, never do. Thus, at fixed effective depth, how the depth is split between block size and iterations decides whether the task is learned. The Deff=16D_{\mathrm{eff}}=16 diagonal shows the same pattern more weakly, with 4×44\times 4 and 2×82\times 8 solving the task in two of five seeds while 8×28\times 2 and the untied 16×116\times 1 never do. Indeed, at learning rate 10−310^{-3}, no untied model solves the task at any depth from 22 to 3232 layers. Effective depth still matters, since no configuration at or below Deff=8D_{\mathrm{eff}}=8 solves the task. This gap does not reflect undertraining, since the untied 3232-layer model’s training loss changes by less than 0.030.03 between the end of the hop curriculum at 3030k steps and the end of training at 100100k (App. A).

Learning rate.

Every run in Figure 3 uses η=10−3\eta=10^{-3}, the looped model’s learning rate. But this may unfairly penalize the untied model, which may suit a different rate. Slowing down to η=3×10−4\eta=3{\times}10^{-4}, we find the untied 3232-layer model now solves the task in four of five seeds, and even the untied 1616-layer model solves it in one seed (Table 1). The 4×84\times 8 looped model still solves in every seed, and reaches the solution sooner on average (4545k training steps against 5555k). Slowing down further to η=10−4\eta=10^{-4}, both models solve in only one of five seeds. Thus, the looped model learns the task over a wider range of learning rates, extending to faster rates at which the untied model fails.

Intermediate supervision.

We find the untied model can also solve the task when we additionally supervise its intermediate layers. Specifically, we revert to η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} and add a next-token loss at layers 88, 1616 and 2424 of the untied 3232-layer model, each read out through the shared unembedding, keeping everything else fixed. In this setup, the untied model solves the task in two of five seeds (Table 1, Fig. A2d).

Longer chains.

On a cycle of N=16N=16 nodes, any hop beyond H=8H=8 can also be reached by walking N−HN-H steps backward, so solving all 1515 hops takes at most 88 sequential steps (§3.1). To test longer chains, we repeat the comparison at N=32N=32, where reaching hop H≤15H\leq 15 takes HH steps, using η=3×10−4\eta=3{\times}10^{-4} (the rate at which both families learn the N=16N=16 task). The untied 3232-layer model never gets past the first hop in any of its three seeds, while the looped 4×84\times 8 model, with an eighth of the parameters, does at least solve the first six hops in one of three seeds (Table 1, Fig. A4).

5 Looped models build a staircase (and use it)

Having established that untied models can also solve the task, albeit only with a lower learning rate or auxiliary supervision, we ask whether they solve it in the same way as looped models. The nature of the task, with its precisely defined intermediate states, provides a unique opportunity to answer this directly, by tracing where in the network each (intermediate) node becomes decodable (§3.4).

Solution structures.

We examine how each model steps through the H=4H=4 solution (if at all) in Figure 4. The looped 4×84\times 8 model reveals successive intermediate nodes a few layers apart, gradually reaching the final answer node by layer 1616 (a). The untied 3232-layer model trained at the same learning rate, however, does not solve the task, and beyond the start node at most one hop ever becomes decodable (b). At the lower learning rate that lets the untied model solve the task (§4), no node beyond the start becomes decodable for the first 2525 layers and then, in a sudden flurry, all three intermediate nodes and the answer become decodable between layer 2626 and 3030 (c). Finally, with the auxiliary loss of §4, the untied model builds a staircase resembling that of the looped model, but with non-uniform step sizes (d). The same holds at H=8H=8 (Figure 1) and across seeds (App. B).

Hopping within an iteration budget.

It is often purported that a looped model consumes one iteration per well-defined step of an algorithm (Giannou et al., 2023; Saunshi et al., 2025; Kohli et al., 2026). Here, we put this to the test by checking whether hop hh indeed becomes decodable at iteration hh, in models whose iteration budget TT exceeds, equals, or falls short of the H=8H=8 required hops of the task (Figure 5).

With more iterations than hops (T>HT>H), the 2×162\times 16 model advances about one hop per iteration in two of three seeds and finishes by iteration 1212 of 1616, and no further hop becomes decodable in the spare iterations (a). The third seed actually reaches the answer by iteration 1010, although hops 22 to 77 never become decodable (App. C). With as many iterations as hops (T=HT=H), the 4×84\times 8 model roughly follows the identity line in all three seeds (b). However, it needs about two iterations to make the first hop, and later makes two hops within a single iteration, so the walk still ends by iteration 88. With fewer iterations than hops (T<HT<H), the 8×48\times 4 model makes several hops within single iterations (!) to reach the answer after its fourth and final iteration (c). At H=12H=12, where four backward steps would reach the answer, the 2×162\times 16 model still makes every forward hop in turn (App. C, Fig. A3). Thus, in most seeds, a looped model takes about one hop per iteration when its budget allows, and packs several hops into an iteration when it does not.

Logit lens and causal interventions.

While probes reveal information that a model can represent linearly, they do not guarantee that the model actually uses it. To test this, we first apply the model’s own output head after each iteration and ask which node it would have written had that been the final iteration, i.e., the logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020). In the 4×84\times 8 model, the head writes the node of hop tt after iteration tt, with probability rising from 0.530.53 at hop 44 to 1.001.00 at hop 77 (Figure 6a). This mirrors the probe staircase of Figure 5, with one interesting difference. The head never puts more than 0.100.10 of its probability on nodes the walk has already passed, so the area under the staircase is white, whereas a probe still decodes each passed node at least half its peak selectivity for about two more iterations (cf. Figure 1). Thus, a passed node fades from the residual stream gradually while the head stops writing it at once, which suggests that the head reads only the current node from a stream that still holds earlier ones.

We also perform causal interventions (Figure 6c), running the model on a second, donor prompt that asks about the same permutation from a different start node. Specifically, we copy the donor’s states at the two answer token positions into the original run after a given iteration and let the remaining iterations finish (§3.4). If these states are meaningfully used, then the model should finish the donor’s walk and write the donor’s answer. We find that the share of donor answers reaches 1.001.00 once the patch comes after the second iteration in two of three seeds, and after the sixth in the third (Figure 6b), while an untrained model writes neither answer (App. C).

Thus, the model’s own output head can read the staircase and the model completes whichever walk its state holds. One caveat is that the readout tracks every hop in only one seed per iteration budget, and a state copied from a prompt with a different permutation yields the node composed from both walks in only one of five seeds, and in no seed of the 2×162\times 16 model (App. C).

6 Discussion and limitations

Pretrained looped models.

So why did Lu et al. (2025) only find limited evidence of a per-iteration chain in Huginn-3.5B (Geiping et al., 2025)? Part of the answer may be the readout, since Lu et al. decode the state with the logit lens and Huginn’s coda but train no probes, and in our models the lens writes the current node at each iteration in only one seed per iteration budget, whereas linear probes decode every hop in most seeds at H=4H=4 (App. B). The rest may lie in training, since Huginn samples a new number of iterations at each training step and backpropagates through only the last eight, whereas our models are each trained at one budget, with which the number of hops per iteration varies (Figure 5). Our task also has a correct node at every step and trains every hop length, two conditions generic pretraining lacks, so we do not claim the staircase forms without them.

Learnability.

That the untied 3232-layer model solves the task at a slower learning rate or with a next-token loss on its intermediate layers is evidence that it is capable of representing a solution (Table 1). Supervising its intermediate layers also gives it a staircase (Figure 4d), and we leave to future work why tied training reaches the staircase while the untied stack needs intermediate supervision.

Design.

For looped model practitioners, our results at a fixed learning rate show that no model looped fewer than three times solved the task (Figure 3), but a model’s budget need not cover every step of the task, since the 8×48\times 4 model solves it in every seed, and its probed seeds pack several hops into each iteration (Figure 5c). A model with spare iterations could exit once its walk ends (Graves, 2016; Zhu et al., 2025), but running a model that packs hops for more iterations, as Geiping et al. (2025) do for Huginn, need not extend its walk, which we leave untested beyond the trained budget.

Limitations.

First, we test a single synthetic task, dePo, chosen because a per-iteration probe needs a known correct answer at every intermediate step, and although we corroborate the behavioral result at N=32N{=}32 (§4) and concurrent work reports a per-loop rate set by the training budget on group word problems (Zhang et al., 2026), whether the staircase survives on tasks that mix retrieval with computation, or on natural language, is open. Second, our models have at most ∼26{\sim}26 M parameters and loop every layer, so our results concern inductive bias at small scale, and the regime in which Huginn wraps its loop in a prelude and coda (Geiping et al., 2025) and Huginn and Ouro (Zhu et al., 2025) report their largest gains remains untested. Third, the grid in Figure 3 uses a single learning rate, only its 4×84\times 8 and untied 3232-layer models were trained at three rates (Table 1), and we probe the internal states of only four of its configurations.

7 Conclusion

We are now in a position to answer the two questions of §1. First, under identical training at matched effective depth, looped models solve the dePo task while untied models, with eight times the parameters, cannot, and succeed only with a lower learning rate or supervision of their intermediate layers (§4). Second, in most seeds, looped models take about one hop per iteration when their budget allows and pack several hops into an iteration when it does not. Linear probes decode these intermediate states and activation patching shows that the model uses them (§5). Thus, on this task, where every intermediate step has a known answer and the loop’s computation is therefore legible, looped transformers appear to be iterative program learners, which execute an algorithm across their iterations without any supervision of its intermediate steps, making the iteration budget a design parameter for tasks with many sequential steps.

Appendix A Training details

Architecture.

Both families use width d=256d=256, 88 heads of dimension 3232, pre-norm RMSNorm (ϵ=10−5\epsilon=10^{-5}), SwiGLU MLPs of hidden width 704704 and rotary position embeddings. The vocabulary has 1818 tokens, ten digits and eight syntax and special tokens, so nodes 1010 to 1515 take two tokens. Looped models add the iteration embedding τt\tau_{t} before each iteration and zero-initialize the attention and MLP output projections of their block (Kohli et al., 2026), while untied models keep the default initialization. No model has input re-injection, a halting head, a prelude or a coda.

Optimization.

AdamW with β=(0.9,0.95)\beta=(0.9,0.95), ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}, weight decay 10−210^{-2} and gradient clipping at norm 11. The learning rate warms up linearly over 1,0001{,}000 steps to its peak η\eta and then follows a cosine decay to 0.1​η0.1\eta. Every run trains for 100100k steps and is evaluated at its final checkpoint. Each step draws 120120 prompts spread evenly over the hop lengths the curriculum allows at that step (§3.3), left-padded to 200200 tokens. The five queries of a prompt share HH and draw their start nodes independently. At N=32N=32 the peak rate is 3×10−43\times 10^{-4}, the warm-up 2,0002{,}000 steps and the context 384384 tokens, with three seeds per model and four for the untied 44-layer control.

Evaluation during training.

Every 44k steps we score 8,0008{,}000 fresh prompts from a held-out generator seed (about 533533 per hop length) on the digits of the last query’s answer, under teacher forcing. Because the queries of a prompt share HH and can repeat a start node, a model that copies earlier answers of the prompt scores about 0.360.36 on this measure, well below the 0.80.8 that defines a solve.

Seeds and hardware.

Seeds are 4242 to 4646, and the untied 44-layer control at N=32N{=}32 also uses seed 4747. The seed sets the initialization, the batch order and the training data, and every cell shares one evaluation seed. Runs were trained on NVIDIA H200 and A40 GPUs. Training is deterministic on a given GPU type, but the same seed on the other type diverges within the first few hundred steps and, for some looped seeds, ends at a different solved-chain depth, so we read each cell’s count as a sample of its seeds.

Compute parity and undertraining.

At matched DeffD_{\mathrm{eff}}, looped and untied models perform the same number of layer evaluations per step and share the step budget, schedule, batch size and hop curriculum, so their FLOPs per step differ only by the addition of τt\tau_{t}. On the same H200 hardware, the looped 4×84\times 8, looped 2×162\times 16 and untied 3232-layer models each train in about 329329 minutes. At η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} the untied 3232-layer model’s training loss falls by only 0.0050.005 to 0.0230.023 between the end of the hop curriculum at 3030k steps and the end of training, while it falls by 0.030.03 to 0.070.07 in every looped seed that solves the task (Fig. A1).

Appendix B Probing details

Probe protocols.

Every probe reads the residual stream at the query position of 5,0005{,}000 evaluation prompts with five queries each (25,00025{,}000 query rows), and one linear probe Linear⁡(d,N)\mathrm{Linear}(d,N) is fitted per state level and hop, for 3030 epochs with AdamW (learning rate 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 10−410^{-4}, batch size 256256). A 3232-layer computation has 3333 state levels, the embedding and the state after each layer. The prompt-disjoint protocol of §3.4 splits the prompts 4,000/1,0004{,}000/1{,}000 and fits the shuffled-label control on the training prompts only. An earlier protocol splits the 25,00025{,}000 query rows at random 80:2080{:}20, so queries of one prompt can fall on both sides, and reads looped models only at the end of each iteration (99 levels for 4×84\times 8, 1717 for 2×162\times 16). Figs. 1 and 5, Fig. 4(a, c) and Fig. A2(c, e) use prompt-disjoint probes, as does the seed-4242 re-probe in Fig. A2(a). Fig. 4(b, d), the other runs of Fig. A2(a, b, d), Fig. A3 and Fig. A5(a) use the row split. Every accuracy reported with the probes is full-answer accuracy on the first query of each of the 5,0005{,}000 prompts (§3.3).

Every seed.

Fig. A2 and Table A1 give the H=4H{=}4 onsets of every probed seed of the four conditions in Fig. 4, and of the looped 4×84\times 8 model at the lower rate. The auxiliary-loss condition was probed in the two of its five seeds that solve the task. In every looped seed the decodable hops appear in hop order, and the answer first becomes decodable in iteration 44 to 88 at η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} and in iteration 44 to 66 at 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4}. Hop 33 of seed 4646 at 10−310^{-3}, which solves the task on the training-time evaluation but answers 65%65\% of first queries, never reaches selectivity 0.50.5. In the untied model at 10−310^{-3}, where no seed solves the task (full-answer accuracy 0.070.07 to 0.170.17), at most hop 11 becomes decodable, at layer 2727 or later. At 3×10−43{\times}10^{-4} every hop of the untied model becomes decodable from layer 2525 on, apart from hop 11 of seed 4343 at layer 1717, and with the auxiliary loss from layer 1010 or 1616 on.

Retention.

After its peak, a hop’s selectivity stays at or above half that peak for a number of further iterations, which we call its retention. In the looped 4×84\times 8 model at H=8H{=}8, averaged over hops 11 to 77 (the answer has no iterations left), retention is 2.22.2 iterations for the three seeds at η=3×10−4\eta=3{\times}10^{-4} (Fig. 1) and 2.62.6 for the prompt-disjoint re-probe of seed 4242 at 10−310^{-3}, both read per layer and converted to iterations, and 1.71.7 for seeds 4242 to 4545 at 10−310^{-3} under the row split, read per iteration.

Sanity controls.

Running the same probes (row split, H=4H{=}4) on an untrained looped 4×84\times 8 model gives accuracies within 0.0080.008 of chance in every cell, so the probe signal comes from the trained weights. Probes retrained on shuffled labels (Hewitt and Liang, 2019) never exceed accuracy 0.190.19 in any cell of either protocol (chance 1/161/16). Stopped after the last iteration, the logit lens of §3.4 reproduces the model’s own full-answer accuracy exactly in all 1414 probed runs of the models in Fig. 5 at H=8H{=}8 and all 1010 at H=4H{=}4, and an untrained model never writes a node under the lens (probability at most 0.0020.002).

Appendix C Additional controls

Forward walk.

At H=12H{=}12 the answer is also four backward steps from the start. Probes on the looped 2×162\times 16 model (seed 4242, η=10−3\eta=10^{-3}, row split, 15,00015{,}000 queries) decode each of the twelve forward-walk nodes πd​(s)\pi^{d}(s), d=1,…,12d=1,\ldots,12, at peak selectivity 0.920.92 to 0.960.96, with the peak iteration rising from 44 at the second node to 1616 at the twelfth (the first node peaks at iteration 77), while the three nodes of the backward route peak at 0.290.29 (Fig. A3). The same pattern holds at H=10H{=}10.

N=32N{=}32.

Every run trains for 100100k steps at η=3×10−4\eta=3{\times}10^{-4} with a 384384-token context (Fig. A4). Solved-chain depths at the final step are 66, 00 and 11 for the looped 4×84\times 8 model (seeds 4242 to 4444) and 11 in every seed of the untied 3232-layer model. An untied 44-layer model, with about as many parameters as the looped model, reaches at most H⋆=1H^{\star}{=}1 in four seeds. Since H≤15<N/2H\leq 15<N/2, no query admits a backward walk shorter than the forward one.

A seed with weak middle hops.

Seed 4444 of the looped 2×162\times 16 model at η=10−3\eta=10^{-3}, the third seed of Fig. 5(a), answers the H=4H{=}4 task (full-answer accuracy 0.9590.959) while hops 22 and 33 stay below selectivity 0.50.5 (Fig. A5a). Its peak selectivity for hops 11 to 33 and the answer is 0.800.80, 0.330.33, 0.300.30 and 0.840.84, against 0.950.95, 0.960.96, 0.960.96 and 0.970.97 for seed 4242. Under the logit lens, seed 4444 never writes hop 22 or 33 alone, and until iteration 1313 it spreads its probability over hops 22 and 33 and the answer (0.280.28 each at iteration 1313), and it writes the answer with probability 0.910.91 only after the last iteration, while seed 4242 writes hop 22, hop 33 and the answer in turn, at peak probabilities 0.530.53, 0.930.93 and 1.001.00 (Fig. A5b, c). At H=8H{=}8 the same seed leaves hops 22 to 77 undecodable while answering 99%99\% of first queries.

Logit lens, every seed.

We apply the full-node lens at H=8H{=}8 to the checkpoints of Fig. 5, on 5,0005{,}000 prompts each. In one seed per iteration budget the head writes the node the walk has reached, as the 4×84\times 8 seed of Fig. 6(a) writes hop tt after iteration tt (0.530.53 to 1.001.00 for hops 44 to 77), seed 4242 of the 2×162\times 16 model writes hop 66 after iteration 88 (0.770.77) and hop 77 after iterations 1010 to 1212 (up to 0.980.98), and seed 4343 of the 8×48\times 4 model writes hop 44 after iteration 22 (0.460.46) and hop 66 after iteration 33 (0.410.41). In the other seeds the head writes only the answer, gives the nodes the walk has passed almost no probability, and reaches lens accuracy 0.90.9 only after the last iteration when T≤HT\leq H, and after iteration 1010 (seed 4646) or 1313 (seed 4444) in the 2×162\times 16 model.

Activation patching, every seed.

We score all five queries of 400400 prompt pairs, with earlier answers teacher forced, for the looped 4×84\times 8 model at H=6H{=}6, and of 300300 pairs for the 2×162\times 16 model at H=8H{=}8. With a shared permutation, every answer is the donor’s once the patch comes after the second iteration in seeds 4343 and 4444, and after the sixth in seed 4242 (Fig. A6a). Of the two 4×84\times 8 seeds the figure omits, seed 4545 gives 0.970.97 after the second iteration and at least 0.9980.998 thereafter, and seed 4646, which answers 76%76\% of queries without patching, gives 0.460.46 to 0.700.70. With different permutations, the node composed from both walks rises above chance only in seed 4242, to 0.190.19 after iteration 55, and stays at or below 0.060.06 in the four other 4×84\times 8 seeds (Fig. A6b) and in every seed of the 2×162\times 16 model. An untrained model writes neither answer in either test. Patching only the readout position moves the first digit, but the second digit of a two-digit answer then becomes the donor’s in under a tenth of cases, so we also patch the first answer digit.

Iteration-embedding ablation.

Retraining the looped 4×84\times 8 model at η=10−3\eta=10^{-3} without the iteration embedding τt\tau_{t} (Xu and Sato, 2025) leaves three of four seeds solving the task, against five of five with it. Since the two conditions have different numbers of seeds, we do not compare their solve rates. In a prompt-disjoint re-probe at H=4H{=}4 and H=8H{=}8, every hop of the three solving seeds becomes decodable, in hop order.
